analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel economy standards to 35 mpg by 2018 with steady 4% annual increases.
analysis.headline: The Fuel Economy Reform Act attracted 154 bipartisan cosponsors in 2007, but the House Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on it, and it died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised federal fuel economy requirements for cars and light trucks, requiring roughly 4% higher miles-per-gallon standards each year so that new vehicles averaged at least 35 mpg by 2018. It also tightened the definition of an automobile to cover vehicles up to 10,000 pounds, closing a gap that let some heavier vehicles avoid fuel economy rules. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary drivers would benefit through lower gasoline spending, since the bill targeted rising fuel costs by requiring vehicles to go farther on each gallon. The bill's own findings cite roughly $500,000 per minute flowing abroad for oil imports at $60 per barrel, framing the standards as a way to keep more of that money in American workers' pockets and the domestic economy.

how_it_helps.text: Requires average fuel economy to reach at least 35 miles per gallon by model year 2018, with a floor of 27.5 mpg for model year 2012 and at least a 4% annual increase thereafter.
Expands the definition of 'automobile' to cover all vehicles up to 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, bringing more pickups and larger vehicles under fuel economy rules.

The bill's findings argue that transportation accounts for two-thirds of domestic oil use, that fuel economy stagnated after 1987 while horsepower and vehicle size grew, and that higher standards would reduce oil imports and the money sent abroad for them.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, led by Detroit's Big Three, would bear the cost of retooling to meet higher mpg standards, and consumers could face higher vehicle prices if those costs are passed on. The bill's findings acknowledge the domestic industry's vulnerability, noting that sustained high gasoline prices were projected to shrink Big Three profits by $7 billion and put nearly 300,000 jobs at risk.

drawbacks.text: Higher compliance costs for automakers could translate into more expensive new vehicles for consumers, hitting lower-income buyers hardest since they are most likely to purchase used or budget vehicles.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised large savings at the pump and reduced dependence on foreign oil, weighed against higher vehicle prices and real adjustment pressure on the domestic auto industry, which the bill itself acknowledged faced shrinking profits and job losses in a high-price environment. The 4% annual ramp with a cost-effectiveness escape clause gave the Transportation Secretary limited flexibility if standards proved unachievable or uneconomic, which partially blunted the compliance shock to automakers.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee referred the bill to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee in March 2007, and no further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on March 13, 2007, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Republicans such as Todd Platts, Mark Kirk, and Christopher Shays.
The bill accumulated 154 cosponsors, 132 Democrats and 22 Republicans.

Despite this broad, bipartisan backing, the House Energy and Commerce Committee never reported the bill out, and it never received a floor vote in either chamber before the 110th Congress concluded on January 3, 2009.

Separately, Congress did enact higher fuel economy requirements in the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007, which became law in December 2007 and required a fleetwide average of 35 mpg by 2020, a slower timeline than this bill's 2018 target.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers—especially the Detroit Three—benefited from the bill's failure, since it died before committee action while the slower 35 mpg-by-2020 timeline in the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 became the binding standard instead. Consumers waited years longer for the fuel savings the bill would have delivered sooner.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fuel Economy Reform Act on March 13, 2007 and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 154 House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support with 132 Democrats and 22 Republicans.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on March 13, 2007, taking no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Auto industry and allied members of Congress
against.what_they_did: Successfully preserved the weaker 35 mpg-by-2020 standard from the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 instead of the faster 35 mpg-by-2018 ramp, and the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 132 of the 154 cosponsors were Democrats and 22 were Republicans, and no vote ever occurred to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have forced faster and steeper fuel economy gains than the industry wanted, requiring retooling and redesign investment years ahead of the pace ultimately written into law in December 2007. Because it would have cut gasoline spending for drivers at the cost of compliance for manufacturers, the industry's interest ran against the bill's consumer benefit.

Higher fuel economy would reduce gasoline demand over time, cutting the volume of oil and refined product the bill's findings valued at roughly $500,000 per minute of import spending. Reduced fuel sales run against drivers' interest in lower gas bills.

New-vehicle buyers would save on gasoline over the life of the car, with standards reaching 35 mpg by 2018 instead of 2020 under the law that actually passed. The cost shows up as somewhat higher sticker prices.
